title: How Vision Works
sub: The Science of Seeing · Grades 5–8 · Science · 30 minutes
objective: Students will understand the basic anatomy of the eye, explain how the brain processes visual information, and analyze why specific optical illusions exploit limitations in the visual system.
materials: **Eye anatomy diagram** — included at end of this document
**Blind spot test cards** — included at end of this document
**Optical Illusions — Use the Mini Museum Perception Lab:** minimuseumproject.org/exhibitions/seeing-is-deceiving/illusions
connection: **Option 1 — Visit:** The 1904 Monarch Stereoscope demonstrates binocular vision. Each Keystone view card has two slightly different photographs — one for each eye. Your visual cortex fuses them into a single 3D scene.

steps.title: The Blind Spot Experiment
script: **Setup:** Distribute blind spot test cards. Instructions: (1) Close left eye, (2) Hold card at arm’s length, focus on + with right eye, (3) Slowly bring card closer — the dot will disappear!

screen.question: Slowly bring card closer — the dot will disappear!

steps.purpose: Every student finds their own blind spot before any explanation.

steps.title: What does this tell us?
script: “The dot didn’t actually disappear — your brain just can’t see it. You have a REAL blind spot where the optic nerve connects. Your brain usually fills in this gap so you never notice. What does this tell us about how we see?”

steps.title: The Eye as a Camera
script: **Part 1: The Eye as a Camera (4 min)** — Using eye diagram, explain path of light:
**1. Cornea** — Clear outer layer that bends (refracts) light
**2. Pupil** — Opening that controls how much light enters (like camera aperture)
**3. Lens** — Focuses light onto the back of the eye
**4. Retina** — Light-sensitive layer with *rods* (light/dark, peripheral) and *cones* (color, center)
**5. Optic nerve** — Carries electrical signals to brain (location of blind spot!)

steps.title: The Brain’s Role
script: **Part 2: The Brain’s Role (3 min)**

“Your eyes don’t ‘see’ anything. They just collect light and convert it to electrical signals. Your BRAIN creates the image. The retinal image is upside-down — your brain flips it. Your brain fills in gaps and makes predictions. Processing happens in the visual cortex at the back of your brain.”
steps.purpose: The eye collects light; the brain makes the picture.
students: The retinal image is upside-down — your brain flips it.
Your brain fills in gaps and makes predictions.

steps.title: Why This Matters
script: **Part 3: Why This Matters (3 min)** — Illusions exploit these processes:
**Eye-based:** Afterimages (tire out cones), peripheral motion (rods vs. cones)
**Brain-based:** Size illusions (context clues), ambiguous figures (brain picks interpretation)

steps.title: Where does it happen?
script: **Illusion 1: Color Afterimage** — *What:* See opposite colors *Why:* Cone cells fatigue; opposite cones fire stronger *Location:* Retina (eye-based)
**Illusion 2: Hermann Grid** — *What:* See dots that aren’t there *Why:* Lateral inhibition — edge cells suppress neighbors *Location:* Retina + early processing
**Illusion 3: Müller-Lyer** — *What:* One line looks longer *Why:* Brain interprets arrows as depth cues *Location:* Visual cortex (brain-based)
**Illusion 4: Stereoscope** — *What:* Depth from flat images *Why:* Each eye sees different image; brain combines *Location:* Visual cortex

steps.title: Connection to Critical Thinking
script: “Your visual system is sophisticated — but it has real limitations. Every illusion teaches us something about how we see. If your brain can be fooled by simple lines and colors, what else might it misinterpret? This is why scientists don’t just trust what they see — they measure, test, and verify.”
